Wiring the perfboard

From the breadboard to the board that goes in the case, written for someone who has never soldered before. It starts with what everything is and how to make a good joint, then goes one small step at a time. Each step has a picture of the board as it should look when the step is done, and a hole map that names every hole used, by its column (A–X) and row (1–18), as printed on the board. Allow about four hours, over a few sittings if you like.

1

What you are building

⏱ 5 min read

On the breadboard, everything was pushed in with jumper wires. That is perfect for testing, but the wires can wiggle loose, and it doesn't fit in the case. This guide moves exactly the same connections onto a small board where they are soldered: joined with melted metal, so they stay put for years.

The board

The board is a perfboard (also called a prototype board): a sheet of fibreglass with a grid of small holes, 2.54 mm apart. That is a tenth of an inch, the same spacing as the pins on the ESP32, so its pins line up with the holes.

Each hole has a shiny metal ring around it on both faces of the board, called a pad. On your board the holes are also plated: metal lines the inside of each hole, joining its top and bottom pads.

The most important thing to know: the holes are not connected to each other. A blank perfboard does nothing. Every connection is one you make, with solder and bits of wire. That is what this guide walks you through.

What goes on it

  • Two sockets the ESP32 plugs into, so you can take it out again later.
  • Three power rails: long bare wires along the back of the board that carry 5 V, 3.3 V and ground to everything.
  • Short bridges: little bare wires that connect each ESP32 pin to a free hole beside it, where that pin's wire goes.
  • Three links: covered wires that connect the ESP32's own power pins to the rails.
  • One capacitor, which steadies the power for the loudspeaker's amplifier.
  • Wires out to every part of the clock: the displays, the amplifier, the clock module, the buttons and lights, and the battery boards.

Each step below has a picture of what the board should look like when the step is done, and a hole map showing exactly which holes to use. Don't rush: if you are new to soldering, the whole board takes about four hours, and it is fine to spread it over a few evenings.

2

Words you will see

⏱ 5 min read

Soldering has its own words. Here is every one this guide uses, in plain terms. Come back to this list whenever a word is unfamiliar.

Solder
A soft metal wire that melts at about 190–220 °C. When it cools it holds parts together and carries electricity. Use thin (0.6–0.8 mm) solder with "rosin core" or "flux core" in its name.
Soldering iron
A pen-shaped heater. Its metal tip gets hot enough to melt solder; the rest of the metal near the tip is hot too.
Joint
One spot where solder joins two things, for example a wire and a pad.
Pad
The metal ring round a hole. Solder sticks to pads; it doesn't stick to the green board.
Lead
Said "leed": a metal leg on a part, like the two legs on the capacitor.
Flux
A cleaning paste or liquid that helps solder flow and stick. There is already some inside your solder; a flux pen adds more when a joint won't flow.
Tinning
Coating something with a thin layer of solder before you join it: the iron's tip, or the end of a wire.
Bare wire
Wire with no plastic covering, usually silver-coloured ("tinned copper"). Used for the rails and bridges. Resistor legs you have cut off work too.
Hookup wire
Wire with a plastic covering (the insulation). Stranded wire has many thin strands inside and bends easily; solid wire has one thick strand and stays where you bend it.
AWG
The wire's thickness. A bigger number is a thinner wire: 26 AWG is thin, 22 AWG thicker.
Strip
Remove the plastic covering from the end of a wire, with wire strippers.
Rail
Also called a bus bar or power bus: one long strip of metal that many wires connect to, so they all get the same power. Like a power strip, or the red and blue lines along the edges of the breadboard.
Ground (GND)
The "0 volts" that every part's power comes back to. Every module needs a ground wire as well as its power wire, or it won't work.
3.3 V and 5 V
The two power supplies. The ESP32, displays and sensors use 3.3 V; the amplifier and the ESP32's input use 5 V. Mixing them up can damage parts, so the guide always says which.
Bridge
In this guide: a short piece of bare wire you solder on to connect neighbouring holes on purpose. (A solder bridge is the mistake: a blob of solder joining holes that should be separate.)
Link
A piece of covered wire joining two holes that are far apart, on the underside.
Socket / female header
A plastic strip of little metal sockets. The ESP32's pins push into them.
Capacitor
A part that stores a little electricity and lets it out quickly, smoothing the power. The one used here has a + and a − leg and must go in the right way round (its polarity).
Continuity test
The multimeter's beep setting. It beeps when its two probe tips touch things that are connected.
Desoldering braid
Also called solder wick: a flat copper braid. Pressed onto a joint with the iron, it soaks up solder, to fix mistakes.
Flush cutters
Small sharp cutters that snip wire and leads flat against the board.
Top and underside
The top (parts side) is where the sockets, capacitor and wires go in. The underside (solder side) is where you solder them and where the rails and bridges lie.
Anchor
In this guide: one of the few holes where a rail or bridge is soldered when it goes on. The rest of its holes are left open for later.
3

Tools, materials and safety

⏱ 10 min

Get everything together before you start, so you never have to put a hot iron down to go looking for something.

⚠️ Never touch the iron's metal, and always return it to its stand.

Tools

  • Soldering iron with a temperature control, a stand to rest it in, and a damp sponge or a ball of brass wool to clean the tip. A fine conical or small chisel tip.
  • Set it to about 330–350 °C (625–660 °F) for ordinary tin-lead solder, or 350–380 °C (660–715 °F) for lead-free solder.
  • Solder: 0.6–0.8 mm, rosin core. Tin-lead (often labelled 63/37 or 60/40) is the easiest to learn with.
  • Flush cutters and wire strippers (with a 26 AWG notch, or an adjustable one).
  • Multimeter with a continuity (beep) setting.
  • Desoldering braid (solder wick), 2–2.5 mm wide, for fixing mistakes. A flux pen helps too.
  • Something to hold the board: a "helping hands" clamp, a small vice, or a lump of putty. Masking tape or Kapton tape for holding wires in place.
  • A bright lamp and a magnifying glass, or your phone's camera zoomed in, for checking joints.
  • Isopropyl alcohol (rubbing alcohol, 90% or more) and an old toothbrush, for cleaning the board at the end.

Materials

  • The 70 × 50 mm perfboard, 24 × 18 holes. It goes in whole: no cutting. A spare one from the kit for practice.
  • Two 22-way 2.54 mm female headers (sockets). If yours are longer, cut them to 22 with a sharp knife, cutting through the 23rd socket.
  • One 100 µF electrolytic capacitor, 10 V or more.
  • Bare tinned wire, about 0.5–0.6 mm (22–24 AWG), about 30 cm in all.
  • Solid insulated wire, thin (26–30 AWG), about 30 cm, for the three links.
  • Stranded hookup wire, 26 AWG, in several colours (red, orange, black and others), and a little 22 AWG red and black for the power input.
  • The two 220 Ω resistors and one 10 kΩ resistor from the breadboard, and some heat-shrink tubing.

Staying safe

  • The iron's tip is hotter than an oven. Always put it back in its stand, never on the bench. Never touch the metal part, even after it's off: it stays hot for several minutes.
  • Fumes: the smoke is from the flux. Work with a window open or a small fan blowing it away from your face, and don't breathe it in.
  • Wear glasses when you snip leads: the cut-off bits fly.
  • If your solder contains lead, wash your hands after soldering, and don't eat or drink at the bench.
  • Work on something that won't burn: a silicone mat, a tile or a piece of wood.
  • Keep the clock's battery unplugged while you work on the board.
  • Turn the iron off when you take a break and when you finish.
4

Learn to make a good joint (practise first)

⏱ 30 min

Every joint on this board is made the same way. Spend half an hour practising on a spare board from the kit, using cut-off resistor legs or bits of bare wire, before you touch the real one. Twenty practice joints make a huge difference.

  1. Clean and tin the tip. Wipe the hot tip on the damp sponge or brass wool, then touch a little solder to it so it looks shiny all over. A shiny tip passes heat well; a dull grey one doesn't. Do this every few joints.
  2. Push a lead through a hole from the top. Turn the board over so you are looking at the underside, and bend the lead out a little so it can't fall out.
  3. Heat both: touch the tip so it touches the pad and the lead at the same time. Count "one, two".
  4. Feed the solder into the joint from the other side: touch the solder to where the lead meets the pad, not to the iron. It melts and flows around the lead and over the pad. About 3 mm of solder is enough for one joint.
  5. Take the solder away first, then the iron. Keep the board still for 3 seconds while the joint sets.
  6. Look at it. Compare it with the pictures below. Then snip the lead about 1 mm above the joint with the flush cutters.

Fixing a joint

  • Too little, dull or lumpy: touch the iron to it again (add a dab of flux if you have it) until it melts and flows shiny, then take the iron away.
  • Too much, or a bridge: lay the end of the desoldering braid on the solder, press the iron on top of the braid, and wait two seconds: the braid soaks up the solder. Lift both off together, then snip off the used, silvery end of the braid.
  • Most mistakes come from not heating long enough, or from melting the solder on the iron and dabbing it on. Heat the joint, and let the joint melt the solder.
Tip: Practise taking a joint apart with the braid too. Then a mistake on the real board is nothing to worry about.
5

Get to know your board

⏱ 5 min

Every hole has a name, printed on the board: its column letter, A to X, counting from the left, and its row number, 1 to 18, counting from the front. So E1 means column E, row 1.

  1. Hold the board so the numbers count up away from you, with row 1 nearest you and the letters reading A to X from left to right.
  2. Put a small piece of masking tape on the edge nearest you and write FRONT on it. Put another on the top face, in a corner, and write TOP. These two labels save a lot of confusion.
  3. To find a hole, put a finger on its letter and slide it toward you to its row number.

Turning the board over: some steps are done on the underside. Always turn it over left to right, like turning a page, so the FRONT edge stays nearest you. Seen from underneath, column A is then on your right, and the letters read X to A. The underside pictures are drawn that way.

6

Fit the ESP32's sockets

⏱ 20 min

The ESP32 doesn't get soldered to the board: it plugs into two strips of sockets, so you can take it out again. These go on first. The trick is to plug the sockets onto the ESP32 before you solder them, so it holds them exactly the right distance apart.

  1. Push the two 22-way socket strips onto the ESP32's two rows of pins, all the way down.
  2. Lower the ESP32, with its sockets, onto the top of the board so the sockets' legs go into rows 3 and 13, columns B to W. The ESP32's metal-covered end (the antenna end) goes over column B; its USB sockets end over column W. Check: the first leg is in B3 and the last in W3.
  3. Hold the ESP32 down and turn the whole thing over left to right, so it rests on the mat on the ESP32 and you see the underside. (Use putty or a folded cloth to keep it level.)
  4. Solder one leg at each end of each strip: four joints. Heat each for no more than about 3 seconds: the plastic can melt.
  5. Turn it back over and check both strips sit flat on the board. If one doesn't, reheat one of its joints while pressing the strip down gently, then let go of the iron first.
  6. Lift the ESP32 straight up and out of the sockets. Put it somewhere safe.
  7. Turn the board over again and solder the remaining 40 legs. They are short: there's no need to trim them.
Why? You can't put a wire into the same hole as a socket's leg, so each socket leg gets its own joint here, and the module wires join the pins through the bridges and links in the next steps.
✅ Check: Look at all 44 joints in a bright light: each a small shiny cone, none touching its neighbour. Then, with the meter on beep, touch neighbouring legs in each row (B3 and C3, C3 and D3, and so on): none may beep.
7

The three power rails

⏱ 30 min

A rail (or bus bar) is one long bare wire that many wires connect to, so they all share the same power, like a power strip. The breadboard had them too: the long lines along its edges. This board has three, side by side along the back, on the underside: row 16 is 5 V, row 17 is 3.3 V, row 18 is ground. Later, every module's power and ground wire goes into one of these rows.

Lay each bar beside its holes, not across them, as in the drawing above, and solder it only at the six orange holes on the hole map. The other holes stay open: a wire, a link or the capacitor goes into some of them later, and its joint then takes in the bar too.

  1. Turn the board over left to right, so you see the underside with the FRONT edge nearest you. It rests on the sockets.
  2. Cut a piece of bare wire about 65 mm long. Straighten it: hold one end in pliers and pull the other end firmly with another pair (or wrap it round a pencil and pull). A straight bar lies flat and is much easier to solder.
  3. Lay it along row 18, the row nearest the far edge, running along the far side of the pads from column A to column X. Hold it down with a strip of tape across the middle.
  4. Solder it at the six orange holes for row 18: columns C, F, L, P, V, W. For each: touch the iron to the pad and the bar together, feed a little solder, and let it flow round the bar onto the pad. Use only a little: it mustn't fill the hole.
  5. Take the tape off. Snip the ends about 1 mm past the last pads.
  6. Do the same for row 17 (solder at columns A, F, K, Q, U, X), then row 16 (columns B, F, K, P, U, X).
Why? If you soldered every hole, the solder would fill them, and you would have to clear them again for the wires that go in later.
✅ Check: Meter on beep: each rail beeps from end to end (for example A18 to X18; touch the bar itself). Rows 16, 17 and 18 must not beep to each other, and row 16 must not beep to row 15. A beep between two rails means solder is joining them: find it with the light and clear it with braid.
8

The short bridges

⏱ 25 min

Each ESP32 pin sits in a socket leg in row 3 or row 13. A module's wire can't share that hole, so it goes into a free hole two rows away, and a short bare wire on the underside joins the two. That is a bridge. There is one for every ESP32 pin that has a wire; the other pins aren't used.

  1. Board still upside down, FRONT edge nearest you.
  2. Cut a piece of bare wire about 9 mm long and straighten it.
  3. Front bridges, columns E, F, G, H, I, J, K, M, P, Q, R, S, T, U: lay the wire beside the holes of rows 1, 2 and 3 in that column, touching the socket leg's joint in row 3.
  4. Solder it at the two orange holes: in row 3, reheat the socket leg's joint so the bar sinks into it, adding a touch of solder; in row 2, solder the bar to its pad. Leave row 1 open: that hole gets the module's wire later.
  5. Snip the ends. Do the next column. Check each one sits in its own column: it must not touch the bridges either side.
  6. Back bridges, columns E, F, G, H: the same along rows 13, 14 and 15, soldered at the row 13 socket leg (and at row 14 where the hole map shows an orange dot). Leave the other holes open.
Why? Holes in row 1, 14 and 15 are where the module wires go in. Leaving them open now makes the wires easy to fit.
✅ Check: Meter on beep: from each bridge's row 1 pad to its socket leg in row 3, it beeps. Between neighbouring columns (E1 and F1, F1 and G1, and so on), it must not.
9

Three insulated links

⏱ 15 min

The ESP32 has its own power pins, and they need joining to the rails: its 3.3 V pin to the 3.3 V rail, a ground pin to the ground rail, and its 5 V pin to the 5 V rail. These wires cross other bare wires on the way, so they must have a plastic covering: that is what makes them links rather than bridges.

  1. Board still upside down. Use the thin solid insulated wire.
  2. For each link: cut a piece a little longer than the distance on the hole map, and strip about 3 mm from each end.
  3. 3.3 V (orange): C3 to C17. At C3, lay the bare end against the socket leg's joint and reheat the joint so it takes the wire in. At C17, lay the other end on the pad and the row 17 bar and solder them together.
  4. Ground (black): B13 to B18, the same way: onto the socket leg at B13, onto the pad and bar at B18.
  5. 5 V (red): V3 to V16, the same way.
  6. Lay each link flat along its column, away from the pads it passes. A dab of tape or glue keeps it down.
Why? Without these, the ESP32 would get no power from the rails, and its 3.3 V wouldn't reach the modules.
✅ Check: Meter on beep: C3 to any pad on row 17, B13 to row 18, V3 to row 16. Then check again that rows 16, 17 and 18 don't beep to each other.
10

The capacitor

⏱ 10 min

The capacitor is a little store of electricity that smooths the 5 V power when the amplifier suddenly needs more for a loud sound. It has a + leg and a − leg, and they must go in the right way round.

  1. Turn the board top side up, FRONT edge nearest you.
  2. Push the long leg (+) into A16 and the short leg (−), the one on the striped side, into A18, from the top. The stripe faces the back edge.
  3. Push it down until it stands about 1 mm above the board. It has to stay under 11 mm tall.
  4. Turn the board over. Bend each leg out a little so it stays put.
  5. Solder each leg: touch the iron to the pad, the leg and the rail's bar together, so one joint holds all three. Snip the legs to 1 mm.
Tip: Nothing else goes in A17 or B17: the capacitor's body sits over them.
✅ Check: Meter on beep: A16 beeps to row 16, A18 to row 18. Between A16 and A18 you may hear a short chirp that stops: that's the capacitor charging from the meter, and it's fine. A steady beep is not: it means solder is joining the rails.
11

How to fit a module wire

⏱ 5 min read

All the remaining steps fit wires that run out to the clock's parts. Every wire goes in the same way.

  1. Cut it to length. Long enough to reach its part with the board in place in the case and the lid lifted off: about 15 cm for most, 25 cm for the lid and the projector display. Too long is easy to tuck away; too short means starting again.
  2. Strip 3 mm of the covering from the board end, twist the strands, and tin them.
  3. Push it into its hole from the top (the hole maps and tables say which), until the covering touches the board.
  4. Turn the board over. Bend the end over a little toward the bar if the hole is on a rail or bridge.
  5. Solder it. If the hole is on a rail or a bridge, touch the iron to the pad, the wire and the bar together, so one joint holds all three.
  6. Snip the end to about 1 mm.
  7. Label the far end with a flag of masking tape: what it is ("front CLK", "amp GND"…). You will thank yourself later.
  8. Give the wire a gentle tug. It mustn't move.

Colours: use the colours in the tables if you have them. Whatever you have, keep to red for 5 V, orange for 3.3 V and black for ground. Then you can always tell the power wires apart.

Tip: Wires in row 1 leave over the front edge. Wires in rows 14 to 18 leave over the back edge. Keep them flat against the board as they go.

Wires: Lid: buttons, lights and light sensor

⏱ 10–15 min

These go to the lid (see the lid harness below). Fit each wire as in the step above, into the hole in the table.

WirePadESP32 / supply
SnoozeG1GPIO 6
Alarm 1 buttonM1GPIO 8

Light sensorH1GPIO 7

The three lid buttons, both alarm lights and the light sensor share one ground wire: run it to the nearest part, then on from part to part (a short wire from one tab to the next). Only the light sensor needs the 3.3 V wire.

  1. Solder a 220 Ω resistor onto each alarm button's LED + tab, then the light wire onto the resistor's other leg. Slide heat-shrink over the resistor and shrink it with the side of the iron or a lighter held well away.
  2. Solder the 10 kΩ resistor from the light sensor's signal leg (the one with its wire) to its ground leg, and cover it with heat-shrink too.
  3. Each alarm button has four tabs: two for the switch, two for its light. The light's + tab is usually marked; if not, find it with the meter's diode setting (the light glows faintly with the red probe on +).

⏱ 10–15 min

These go to the 5 V boost (or straight to the USB-C breakout without the battery). Fit each wire as in the step above, into the hole in the table.

These two bring power to the board. Use the thicker 22 AWG wire. With the battery, they come from the 5 V booster board's VOUT (red) and GND (black). Without it, they come straight from the USB-C socket board's VBUS (red) and GND (black).

⚠️ Double-check these two before you power anything: red into the 5 V rail (row 16), black into ground (row 18). Swapped, they can damage the ESP32.
20

Check every wire

⏱ 15 min

Before anything goes near power, check the whole board against this map and the pictures. Go wire by wire with a finger on the map.

  1. Every wire is in the hole the tables say, and its far end is labelled.
  2. The power wires: red into row 16 (5 V), orange into row 17 (3.3 V), black into row 18 (ground).
  3. Nothing is in A17 or B17, under the capacitor.

Turn it round

Drag to turn the finished board; scroll or pinch to zoom. "Underside" turns it over left to right, the same way as in your hands.

21

Clean the underside, and protect it

⏱ 20 min

Leftover flux is sticky and can hide tiny solder bridges. Cleaning it off lets you see every joint clearly.

  1. Dip an old toothbrush in isopropyl alcohol and scrub the underside gently, a small area at a time. Wipe with a paper towel. Let it dry for a few minutes.
  2. Look over every joint in a bright light, with a magnifier or your phone's camera zoomed in. Look especially between neighbouring pads: any silver thread of solder joining them must go.
  3. Look for stray wire strands poking out of a joint, and snip them.
  4. Do the beep tests once more: rows 16, 17 and 18 must not beep to each other, and no two neighbouring columns in rows 1 to 3 may beep.
  5. When everything has passed (after the test in the next step is best), cover the underside with Kapton tape, which is heat-proof and thin. Lay strips side by side over the rails and bridges. It stops anything in the case touching the bare wires.
✅ Check: Every beep test passes, and you can't see any solder joining two pads that the hole maps don't join.
22

Plug in the ESP32 and test, one part at a time

⏱ 30–45 min

Now move the ESP32 over from the breadboard and bring the clock back to life, one part at a time, so that if something is wrong you know exactly which wires to look at.

⚠️ Never plug the USB-C power and the ESP32's own USB socket in at the same time.
  1. Unplug all power. Lift the ESP32 off the breadboard, rocking it gently from end to end.
  2. Plug it into the board's sockets: antenna end over column B, USB sockets at column W. Every pin must go into a socket: count 22 in each row.
  3. Connect only the two power-in wires and the front display's four wires. Plug in the USB-C power. Within 30 seconds the front display shows the time.
  4. If anything gets hot or smells hot, unplug at once and see "If something doesn't work" below.
  5. Unplug the power. Connect the next part: projector display, then the amplifier, the clock module, the lid, button B and the battery boards. Power up after each one and run that part's test from the breadboard guide.
  6. Open the clock's web page: its status shows the clock module found, and with the battery boards, a Battery line.
✅ Check: Everything that worked on the breadboard works here.
23

Into the case

⏱ 10 min

The board sits on the four posts at the front right of the base, with the ESP32's USB end toward the right wall and the FRONT edge toward the front.

  1. Lower it onto the posts, then slide it forward until its back edge clears the barrel's bearing block in the back-right corner. About 10 mm of the board then hangs past the front posts.
  2. Press it down until the two hooks on each short side click over its ends.
  3. Route the lid and projector wires up the right side. Leave the battery and clock-module wires along the floor. Keep everything clear of the barrel: it turns.
  4. See the assembly steps for the rest.
24

If something doesn't work

⏱ –

Almost every problem is one joint or one wire. Unplug the power before you touch anything, then:

  • Nothing lights up: check the power-in wires: red in row 16, black in row 18. Beep from the power board's VOUT to any pad on row 16, and from its GND to row 18. Check the 5 V link (V3 to row 16).
  • Something gets hot, or the power supply cuts out: two rails are joined. Beep rows 16, 17 and 18 against each other with the ESP32 out, and look for a solder bridge between them.
  • One part doesn't work: its wires are the only new thing. Beep each one from the part's own pin to its pad on the board, and from that pad to the ESP32 socket leg (through its bridge). One that doesn't beep is a bad joint or a broken wire.
  • A part works sometimes, or the clock restarts at random: usually a dull, lumpy joint on a power or ground wire. Reheat the joints in rows 16 to 18 until they are shiny.
  • A display shows garbage: its CLK and DIO wires are swapped. Swap them at the part's end.
  • Two neighbouring columns beep together: a solder bridge. Clear it with braid.

If you are stuck, the wiring page lists every connection by the module's pin names.
